title: Practical Considerations for the Design, Execution, and Interpretation of Studies Involving Whole-Bone Bending Tests of Rodent Bones
protocol: Place the mouse ventral side up.
Make an incision at the approximate junction of the femur and pelvis on one side with a scalpel (or a razor blade or scissors).
Continue the initial incision dorsally until the hip joint is located.
Apply pressure with the edge of a scalpel to the proximal edge of the femoral head until it pops out of the socket.
Excise additional tissue to free the hindlimb from the remainder of the carcass.
Separate the tibia and femur by inducing flexion at the knee joint.
Move the scalpel in the medial-lateral direction at the anterior surface of the knee to cut through any adjoining tissue, including the ligaments between the bones.
Extend the knee joint if necessary to allow access to the posterior surface for separation.
Be careful to avoid cutting the bone or scraping the articular cartilage.
Separate the femur and tibia.
Remove the hindfoot from the tibia using a flexing motion and medial-lateral sawing on the posterior surface of the joint.
Extend the joint if necessary to expose the anterior surface for easier removal of soft tissue.
Clean all adherent soft tissue from the bones.
If performing four-point bending tests, remove the fibula by cutting near its connection point with sharp scissors.
Wrap isolated and cleaned bones separately in saline-soaked gauze.
Store wrapped bones at -20°C immediately after harvest.
Repeat steps for the other side of the carcass.
Minimize freeze-thaw cycles to preserve bone mechanical properties.
Thaw bones partially for µCT scanning by leaving them at room temperature for 5-10 minutes.
Completely thaw bones only when performing bending tests.
Move the bones from -20°C storage to a cold room or refrigerator at 1-4°C.
Ensure the bones remain in the cold room for 8-12 hours to fully thaw prior to testing.
Set the temperature of the bath to approximately 37°C.
Add the bones to the bath once it reaches 37°C.
Leave the bones in the bath for approximately 1 hour.
Wrap the bones in parafilm prior to scanning to maintain hydration.
Keep all other bones on ice while waiting to be scanned.
Place the bone into a holder to interface with the scanner after wrapping.
Ensure all scanned bones are aligned in the same orientation as consistent alignment will simplify rotation later in the analysis.
Adjust scan settings according to the application of the scan.
Use the following general scan settings for mouse bones: resolution/voxel size 10 µm, pixel size medium (2000 x 1048), filter 0.5 mm aluminum, rotation step 0.7, frame averaging 2.
Perform a flat field correction to minimize artifacts once the x-ray source is on.
Ensure the chamber is empty before performing flat field correction.
Measure the average intensity of the field and adjust it to 60%.
Update the flat field and turn it back on after adjusting to 60%.
Ensure the average intensity is now (86-88%).
Place the holder in the chamber after performing flat-field correction.
Ensure samples are centered and level on the pedestal.
Securely place the pedestal in the chamber.
Close the chamber and ensure the entire bone will be captured.
Obtain a scout view if necessary to confirm full bone capture.
Start the scan once all settings are confirmed.
Re-store bones in saline-soaked gauze at -20°C after scanning.
Select an ROI that captures the entire bone based on its largest cross section.
Set the lower constraint of the thresholding software histogram to 0.
Set the upper constraint of the histogram to the end of the peak data.
Adjust ring artifact reduction settings to 5%.
Adjust beam hardening settings to 20%.
Check misalignment compensation values are within -7 to 7 range.
Rotate the femur so all bones have the same longitudinal orientation.
Rotate the bone so that the cross-sectional orientation of all bones is the same.
Straighten the scan to ensure symmetry is maintained about the central axis.
Save the rotated dataset.
Repeat steps for tibia rotation as described for femur.
Obtain µCT scans and reconstruct them to verify quality for each sample.
Thaw all bones prior to testing.
Randomize the order of bone testing within an experiment.
Ensure bones remain hydrated throughout the testing process.
Select a load cell with appropriate sensitivity and capacity for the specimen.
Install the load cell onto either the top or bottom support of the tester, securing it tightly.
Attach the top loading fixture to the load cell.
Install the bottom fixture onto the bottom support of the tester.
Select a support span length based on the shortest bone in the sample set.
Ensure the support span remains constant for all samples being tested.
Orient the femur between the fixtures with the anterior surface against the support span, excluding the third trochanter on the proximal end and the transition point on the distal end.
Set up four-point bending by aligning and centering the support and loading spans in a 3:1 ratio (e.g., 9 mm support span and 3 mm loading span).
Position the tibia with one support at the tibia/fibula junction and another just after the tibial crest for four-point bending.
Measure the support span distance if performing three-point bending.
Record both loading and support span distances if performing four-point bending, measuring from the center of the loading points.
Place the bone back in saline or rehydrate with a bolus of saline.
Use circular points for loading span selection, with a radius of 0.75 mm.
Ensure all parts of the fixture are tight and free of movement.
Connect the tester to the computer via the module box and load cell channels.
Create a bending test profile with a displacement rate of 0.025 mm/s in the software.
Set a minimum sample frequency of 25 Hz when creating a testing profile.
Create one folder per study group for saving test files.
Select a properly thawed bone.
Measure and record the full length of the bone with calipers.
Load the sample onto the fixtures as shown for three-point bending if testing a femur or four-point bending if testing a tibia.
Change the file name to reflect the specific sample being tested.
Zero the load.
Turn on the mover of the system; ensure it is not in load or displacement control.
Apply a minimal preload to the bone, approximately 0.25 N, to secure its position and prevent rolling.
Ensure the desired bone orientation is maintained.
Hydrate the sample by dousing it generously with saline.
Begin the bending test by selecting Start or Run in the software.
Carefully watch the sample for the entirety of the test.
Note any issues during testing (e.g., rolling, slipping).
Watch for the bone to begin to fracture on the tensile side.
Manually stop the test if failure occurs but displacement continues.
Measure the length from the distal end to the break point using calipers and record it.
Load rotated images into user's software of choice.
Locate and record the top and bottom slices of the bone.
Calculate the difference between the top and bottom slices.
Multiply this value by the scanning voxel size to determine the overall length of the bone in micrometers.
Divide the recorded break length (in micrometers) by voxel size to obtain the number of µCT slices from the distal end of the scan to the break point.
Set the total desired length of the ROI (at least 100 µm).
Find the number of slices this length represents by dividing the length in micrometers by the voxel size.
Divide the total number of ROI slices by 2 and subtract this value from the previously calculated break location to obtain the lower bound of the ROI.
Add the total length of the ROI in slices to the previously calculated value to obtain the upper bound of the ROI.
Select the appropriate ROI based on calculated bounds.
Save the selected ROI.
Normalize force and displacement data using geometric properties obtained from µCT scans.
Calculate stress using Euler-Bernoulli bending stress equations.
Obtain necessary geometric properties from µCT scans for calculations.
Calculate strain using the provided equation where "c" and "L" represent properties from stress calculations, and "d" is displacement recorded during tests.
Calculate stress in four-point bending using the given equation with variables F and I as previously discussed.
Determine "a" for the support span ratio of 3:1 for four-point bending testing.
Measure displacement values (d) recorded by the mechanical tester during tests to calculate strain according to the provided formula.
Determine the centroid of each cross section in µCT scans since the neutral axis passes through the centroid.
Measure "c" with respect to the anterior surface for a femur.
Measure "c" with respect to the medial surface of the bone for a tibia.
Calculate the area moment of inertia about the axis of bending using Equation 5.
Use "dA" as the area of each pixel captured in the µCT scan.
Determine "y" as the calculated distance of each pixel from the neutral axis.
Generate a force-displacement curve before calculating mechanical properties.
Generate a stress-strain curve for analysis.
Examine the curves prior to analysis to spot errors such as bone rolling or slipping.
Remove excess data, including any collected prior to the tester contacting the bone.
Exclude data following failure.
Calculate stiffness using only the elastic region of the force-displacement curve.
Calculate elastic modulus using the slope of only the elastic portion of the stress-strain curve.
Identify the yield point on the force-displacement curve to determine displacement to yield and yield force.
Identify the yield point on the stress-strain curve to determine strain to yield and yield stress.
Calculate a line offset from (0,0) by 0.2% strain but with the same slope as the elastic modulus.
Plot this line on the stress-strain graph.
Define the yield point as the position where the plotted line intercepts the stress-strain curve.
Use the yield stress and strain coordinate to find the analogous force and displacement values.
Calculate stiffness from the force-displacement curve.
Reduce the stiffness by a chosen percentage (5-10%).
Plot a line starting at (0,0) with the slope of this reduced stiffness.
Allow the plotted line to intersect with the force-displacement curve.
The point of intersection will have coordinates representing displacement to yield and yield force.
Calculate ultimate force and ultimate stress by finding the maximum value in respective data sets.
Locate the yield as described in step 8.3.2.
Find displacement to yield and strain to yield values representing displacement or strain to the yield point.
Determine total displacement and total strain values corresponding to the failure point of the sample test.
